newsitem.title: UK: Diana at eye of political storm over landmines.
newsitem.headline: Diana at eye of political storm over landmines.

text.p: Princess Diana was at the centre of a political storm in Britain on Wednesday over her call during a visit to war-torn Angola for a worldwide ban on anti-personnel landmines.

One minister was reported to have said Diana, dubbed the "princess of peace" after she met casualties of Angola's 20-year war, was ill-advised for speaking out on a politically sensitive issue and appearing to be at odds with government policy.

Aides to Prime Minister John Major tried to play down her initiative but a prominent member of his ruling Conservative party rounded on the divorced wife of heir-to-the throne Prince Charles for being "very uninformed".
"The parallel of nuclear weapons comes to mind. The other parallel that comes to my mind is Brigitte Bardot and cats. It doesn't actually add much to the sum of human knowledge.
"This is an important, sophisticated argument. It doesn't help simply to point at the amputees and say how terrible it is," Peter Viggers, who sits on parliament's defence committee, told BBC radio.

Another Conservative, David Howell, told BBC television: "I appreciate that stars and celebrities and public figures should have feelings and should express them, but I think it is important that they should be qualified by the realisation that things are not straightforward."

Diana, who has spoken of her desire to be Britain's "Queen of Hearts" in a roving semi-ambassadorial role, is visiting Angola on behalf of the Red Cross to highlight the human suffering caused by the indiscriminate sowing of landmines.

Her call for an international ban on the "hideous weapons" has caused a stir because Conservatives believe it could be read as endorsement of the policy of the main opposition Labour party, clear favourite to win Britain's forthcoming election.

The government backs a ban on most anti-personnel landmines but says it must be international to be effective. So-called "smart mines" -- that self-destruct after a period of time -- are excluded from government plans.

In contrast, the Red Cross -- and Labour -- want the government to declare a unilateral ban and to destroy all its existing stocks. Pending a global ban, the Ministry of Defence is in the process of scrapping just half its stockpile.

"She was ill-advised and is not being helpful or realistic. Britain is one of the goodies on landmines and we are helping to draw up a sensible worldwide compromise package. We do not need a loose cannon like her," an unnamed minister told The Times newspaper.
Other ministers tried to defuse the controversy, saying the government shared the Red Cross's ultimate goal.

"The government is fully committed to working for a worldwide ban on anti-personnel landmines. We are active internationally to that end and we have imposed a total moratorium on exports," defence procurement minister James Arbuthnot said in a statement.

An aide to Major, asked whether the prime minister viewed Diana's remarks as helpful and whether she had been right to speak out on the issue, would say only that her comments had been "entirely understandable in the context".
Diana's visit marks a major departure from the usual gala events she has attended on behalf of charities since her divorce last August.
